title: Async and Await Basics
oneLiner: Waiting without blocking: async methods and coroutines, await, Task.WhenAll versus asyncio.gather, sequential versus concurrent waits, when each language starts running an async call, and the common mistakes.
keyTakeaway: await pauses a method until a result is ready while other work runs. Start independent operations first and await them together (Task.WhenAll, asyncio.gather) so the waits overlap. A C# async method runs until its first await when called; a Python coroutine doesn't start until it's awaited or scheduled and the event loop gets control.
explanation:
Programs that talk to networks, databases, files or devices spend most of their time waiting. Ordinary code waits by blocking: the thread sits idle until the reply arrives. Asynchronous code instead starts the operation, lets other work run, and resumes when the result is ready. With async/await this reads almost like ordinary top-to-bottom code.

An async method returns a pending result straight away: a Task in C#, a coroutine in Python (which an event loop, the scheduler that runs Python's async code, wraps in a task). Writing await in front of it pauses the current method until the result is ready. The big win comes from starting several operations before awaiting any of them, so their waits overlap.

The languages agree on the idea and differ in details that change the order of events, shown step by step in the lesson: when an async call actually starts running, how the program's entry point starts the machinery, and what happens if you forget to await. Async helps with waiting, not with heavy computation.

This is a first look with runnable samples; there's no graded exercise because the exercise sandbox doesn't allow tasks. Stage 3 goes deeper, and async/await vs Threads in Concurrency & Memory explains what happens underneath.
